\title{Measured Edge-Inference Energy Versus Quality-Driven Carbon, Material, and Workload Effects of AI Defect Inspection in Manufacturing}

\author{Utkarsh~Sengar%
\thanks{U.~Sengar is with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Dharwad, Karnataka 580011, India (e-mail: cs23bt026@iitdh.ac.in).}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Edge deep-learning inspection is often assumed to be environmentally beneficial because it prevents scrap; critics counter that always-on inference consumes electricity. We quantify both sides. A conservation-checked accounting model compares four edge-AI alert policies against two explicit counterfactuals, no inspection and manual end-of-line inspection, in three manufacturing scenarios. It couples defect routing, delay-dependent reworkability, material recovery, operator workload, electricity, amortised edge hardware and field escapes. The alert policies' false-alert rates, repeat alerts and delays are imported, with their confidence intervals, from our measurement study of the same policies, and every other parameter sits in a single ledger with tracked provenance. We measured a PatchCore-style ResNet-18 pipeline at a 30~FPS line rate on an NVIDIA \GpuName{}: it draws \FullTotalPower~W in total and \FullFrameEnergy~J per frame above idle. The edge cell accounts for at most \EdgeShareMax\% of the full policy's carbon footprint and less than 1\% of its benefit over manual inspection. Against manual inspection the median benefit is \PrecMcMedian, \MetalMcMedian{} and \HiValMcMedian{}~\kgce{} per 1{,}000 parts, positive in all \MonteCarloDraws{} Monte Carlo draws, with \EscapeShareMin--\EscapeShareMax\% from avoided field escapes. Alert policy matters more than compute: single-frame thresholding would need tens to hundreds of reviewers, and the full policy saves operator time, electricity and carbon relative to it unless persistence costs more recall than a margin that shrinks to \HiValRecallLossStar{} percentage points for high-value parts.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Sustainable manufacturing, edge AI, industrial anomaly detection, energy measurement, carbon accounting, alarm management, uncertainty analysis.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{A}{utomated} optical inspection with unsupervised anomaly detectors such as PatchCore and PaDiM~\cite{roth2022patchcore,defard2021padim} is now accurate enough on public benchmarks~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} for deployment on edge computers beside production lines. Two opposing sustainability narratives surround these deployments. One holds that inspection is intrinsically ``green'' because intercepted defects are reworked instead of scrapped. The other, prompted by the rapid growth of machine-learning energy use~\cite{strubell2020energy,desislavov2023trends}, asks whether always-on inference erodes those gains. Neither claim is usually quantified for an actual production line, and published estimates rarely separate measured quantities from assumptions. A third factor is usually left out: a detector that alerts on every frame can bury the operators who must act on its alerts.

We ask three questions for a functional unit of 1{,}000 inspected parts:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Magnitude.} How large is the measured electricity and embodied-hardware footprint of an edge inference cell relative to the material, rework, workload and field-escape effects that inspection changes?
\item \emph{Counterfactual.} Against which baseline---no inspection or manual end-of-line inspection---and under which defect prevalence, compute budget and grid intensity does edge AI stop being carbon-beneficial?
\item \emph{Policy.} With identical compute, how do measured alert policies change operator workload and carbon, and how much recall may temporal filtering lose before it stops paying off?
\end{enumerate}

This paper makes four contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item An open, conservation-checked accounting model with explicit counterfactual baselines (no inspection, manual inspection) and four AI alert policies. Every parameter lives in one validated ledger (Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies}) that reports its provenance class (\RegistryMeasuredCount{} measured, \RegistryPaperACount{} imported from our alert-policy study, \RegistryLiteratureCount{} literature, \RegistryOfficialCount{} official dataset, \RegistryAssumptionCount{} scenario assumptions).
\item A line-rate power measurement of a PatchCore-style pipeline with a protocol that respects the refresh limits of on-board GPU power sensors~\cite{yang2024accurate}, including a documented negative result on the NVML energy counter under WSL2.
\item Quantified break-even frontiers (prevalence, edge-cell power, grid intensity, manual-inspection recall), global sensitivity by partial rank correlation, and a weight-robust multi-criteria index.
\item A link between alarm management and sustainability: using measured alert rates, we show that alert policy dominates operator load and that temporal filtering stays carbon-beneficial only within a quantified recall-loss margin.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\emph{Industrial anomaly detection.} MVTec~AD~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} established the standard benchmark; PatchCore~\cite{roth2022patchcore} and PaDiM~\cite{defard2021padim} use pretrained CNN patch features with nearest-neighbour or Gaussian scoring. Our earlier work benchmarks cost-calibrated thresholding~\cite{sengar2026flagship1}. A companion study~\cite{sengar2026paperA} turns PatchCore scores into operator alerts through exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence, machine-state gating, divergence triage and an incident latch, and measures eight policy variants on simulated inspection workloads. On good parts, single-frame thresholding raised \PaperAFaRaw{} false alerts per hour and the full policy \PaperAFaFull{}; a sustained defect produced \PaperAPerDefectRaw{} alerts under thresholding and \PaperAPerDefectFull{} under the full policy, at a mean delay of \PaperADelay{} frames. We import those per-policy measurements, with their confidence intervals, and the study's reviewer service rate.

\emph{Energy of machine learning.} Energy accounting for ML has concentrated on training and data-centre inference~\cite{strubell2020energy,henderson2020towards,desislavov2023trends}. On-board NVIDIA sensors are convenient, but on some architectures they sample only part of the runtime, and they refresh at limited rates~\cite{yang2024accurate}. Long, steady-state measurement windows mitigate both problems.

\emph{Manufacturing material and energy efficiency.} Material production dominates the energy of many products~\cite{gutowski2013energy}, and material efficiency---including yield improvement and scrap avoidance---is a recognised mitigation lever~\cite{allwood2011material,ashby2012materials}. ISO~14040/14044 standardise life-cycle assessment practice~\cite{finkbeiner2006new}. Human visual inspection typically misses 20--30\% of defects~\cite{see2012visual}; this range bounds our manual baseline. We know of no work that places measured edge-inference energy and measured alert loads on the same functional unit as these quality-driven flows.

\section{Accounting Model}
\subsection{Functional Unit, Regimes and Boundary}
The functional unit (FU) is $N=1{,}000$ consecutively produced parts. A line with throughput $\Theta$ [parts/h] needs $T_{FU}=N/\Theta$ hours to produce one FU. The gate-to-gate boundary (Fig.~\ref{fig:boundary}) covers inspection electricity, operator-review or manual-inspection workstations, rework electricity, the embodied carbon of unrecovered scrap, the processing burden of recovered scrap, the amortised embodied carbon of the edge hardware, and the consequences of field escapes. Facility base loads, logistics of good parts and labour-related emissions are identical across regimes, so we exclude them. Electricity carries location-based grid factors.

Six regimes enter the comparison. \emph{N0}: no inspection. \emph{L0}: 100\% manual end-of-line visual inspection with recall $r_{L0}$, discovery delay $d_{L0}$ and $t_{L0}$ seconds per part. \emph{B0--B3}: a continuously running edge AI cell under one of the four alert policies measured in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: single-frame thresholding (B0), exponential smoothing (B1), smoothing with $k$-of-$N$ persistence (B2), and the full policy, which adds an incident latch, machine-state gating and divergence triage (B3). The cell diverts flagged parts automatically and an operator reviews every alert afterwards, so review queues do not delay interception.

\subsection{Defect Routing and Reworkability}
With prevalence $\pi$ the FU contains $D=N\pi$ defects in classes A (reworkable), B (scrap-prone) and C (escape-sensitive) with shares $f_A,f_B,f_C$. A regime with recall $r$ and interception delay $d$ [s] yields
\begin{align}
N_{rw} &= f_A\, r D\, q_{rw}(d), \quad q_{rw}(d) = q_0\, e^{-d/\tau_{rw}}, \label{eq:rw}\\
N_{sc} &= rD - N_{rw}, \qquad N_{esc} = (1-r)D, \label{eq:sc}
\end{align}
where $q_0$ is the zero-delay reworkability and $\tau_{rw}$ the time constant with which a defective part advances into irreversible downstream operations. By construction $N_{rw}+N_{sc}+N_{esc}=D$, and the implementation checks this identity numerically at every evaluation. For L0, $r=r_{L0}$ and $d=d_{L0}$. For an AI policy $t$, $d=d_t/f_{cam}$ with the measured mean delay $d_t$ in frames, and $r=r_{AI}-\delta_r$, where $r_{AI}$ is the detector's recall and $\delta_r$ is a recall loss charged only to the persistence policies B2 and B3. The companion study observed no such loss---all four policies detected every sustained defect---so $\delta_r$ is centred on zero and studied as a break-even parameter.

\subsection{Material, Workload and Energy}
Scrap mass is $M_{gr}=N_{sc}m$ for part mass $m$, of which $M_{rec}=\eta M_{gr}$ is recovered and $M_{loss}=(1-\eta)M_{gr}$ lost. We adopt the operator-load model of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: every alert reaches the review queue. For policy $t$ the false-alert rate is $\lambda_{FA}=\lambda_t+g\,b_t$, where $\lambda_t$ [1/h] is the measured rate on good parts, $b_t$ the measured alerts per glare burst and $g$ [1/h] the rate of glare bursts. Each detected defect raises $a_t$ alerts. The operator therefore reviews $n_{ev}=\lambda_{FA}T_{FU}+a_t\,rD$ alerts per FU, giving
\begin{equation}
H = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600}\ \text{[h/FU]}, \qquad \rho = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600\, T_{FU}},
\end{equation}
where $t_{review}$ [s] is the time to review one alert and $\rho$ is the utilisation of a single operator; for L0, $H=N t_{L0}/3600$ and $\rho=\Theta t_{L0}/3600$; for N0, $H=0$. Electricity per FU [kWh] is
\begin{align}
E_{edge} &= (P_{idle}+P_{active}+P_{host})\,T_{FU}/1000, \\
E_{rev} &= H\,P_{station}/1000, \qquad E_{rw} = N_{rw}\,e_{rw},
\end{align}
with $E_{edge}=0$ for N0 and L0. $P_{idle}$ and $P_{active}$ are the measured GPU powers at the camera rate (Section~\ref{sec:measure}); $P_{host}$ covers host computer, camera and lighting, which NVML cannot observe.

\subsection{Carbon}
Carbon per FU is the sum of seven non-negative components,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
C ={}& M_{loss}EF_{mat} + M_{rec}EF_{rec} + \gamma\,(E_{rw}+E_{rev}+E_{edge}) \\
& + C_{hw}T_{FU}/L_{hw} + N_{esc}\,(m\,EF_{mat}+c_{ret}) \\
& + \kappa f_C N_{esc}\, m\,EF_{mat},
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where $EF_{mat}$ is the cradle-to-gate material factor, $EF_{rec}$ the processing burden of recovered scrap, $\gamma$ the grid intensity, $C_{hw}$ and $L_{hw}$ the embodied carbon and service life of the edge computer (the hardware term, like $E_{edge}$, is zero for N0 and L0), and each escaped part is replaced (its material is lost) and returned ($c_{ret}$); class-C escapes add collateral damage $\kappa\, m\,EF_{mat}$. Escape consequences scale with the part; they are not a fixed penalty. For any regime $p$ and baseline $b$, savings are $\Delta X = X_b - X_p$ for $X\in\{M_{loss},E,C,H\}$. The carbon saving $\Delta C$ decomposes exactly into the seven component differences, which we verify to machine precision.

\subsection{Sustainability Quality Index}
For the four dimensions, all non-negative by construction, the bounded sub-indicators are $S_X=(X_b-X_p)/\max(X_b,X_p)\in[-1,1]$ ($S_X=0$ when $X_b=X_p=0$), and $\mathrm{SQI}=\sum_X w_X S_X$ with four stakeholder weight profiles (balanced, material-, carbon- and human-centred). Any scalarisation embeds value judgements, so we also report the share of the whole weight simplex (uniform Dirichlet samples) for which $\mathrm{SQI}>0$.

\subsection{Parameters and Uncertainty}
Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies} list all \RegistryEntries{} parameter entries with central value, bounds, unit, provenance class and source; both tables are generated from the ledger file and cannot drift from the code. The alert-policy entries are the means and 95\% bootstrap intervals reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, imported from one pinned revision of its artifact; the review time is centred on its service rate of \PaperAMu{} reviews/h and the glare rate on its assumed \PaperAGlareRate{} bursts/h. Grid intensity is centred on the EU-27 2023 value (0.242~kg/kWh~\cite{ember2024}), with the Indian FY2022--23 weighted average (0.716~kg/kWh~\cite{cea2024}) as upper bound. Most other parameters are scenario assumptions; the analysis is built to show which of them matter. We propagate uncertainty with \MonteCarloDraws{} independent triangular draws on the ledger bounds (seed 42) and rank global sensitivity with partial rank correlation coefficients (PRCC)~\cite{marino2008methodology}. Brent's method solves each break-even frontier ($\Delta C=0$) on a physically bounded interval; where $\Delta C$ does not change sign, we report ``none'' together with that sign.

\section{Edge Inference Power Measurement}
\label{sec:measure}
\subsection{Workload and Protocol}
The workload is a PatchCore-style detector configured as in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: a ResNet-18 backbone, layer-2 and layer-3 features pooled to $28\times28\times384$ patch descriptors, and exact 1-nearest-neighbour search against a $\PaperABank\times384$ memory bank, for $224\times224$ RGB frames at batch size~1 in FP32 (PyTorch \TorchVersion, CUDA \CudaRuntime, driver \GpuDriver, WSL2). Weights are randomly initialised, because inference cost does not depend on weight values. We measured four cumulative stages: the model alone; plus score thresholding; plus a temporal policy (exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence and cooldown); and the full pipeline with SQLite write-ahead-log event persistence and JSON serialisation. Each stage ran paced at the line rate of \BenchFps~FPS for \BenchWindow~s windows, in \BenchRepeats{} repeats with a seeded random stage order, and a 15~s idle window preceded every repeat. We sampled GPU power with NVML at 20~Hz and integrated it over each window; every stage window contains at least \StageReadingsMin{} distinct sensor readings (idle windows at least \IdleReadingsMin). We also logged the NVML cumulative energy counter but do not use it: under WSL2 it reported \CounterIdleMinW--\CounterIdleMaxW~W at idle, inconsistent with the power sensor. We report the median across repeats, with the minimum and maximum as bounds. The GPU also drives the host desktop; windows disturbed by desktop activity remain in the bounds and in the raw data.

\subsection{Results}
Fig.~\ref{fig:energy} shows that at \BenchFps~FPS the stages are indistinguishable: median total power ranges over \StageSpreadW~W, against an idle level of \IdlePower~W. The full pipeline draws \FullTotalPower~W in total and \FullActivePower~W above idle (bounds \FullActivePowerMin--\FullActivePowerMax~W), or \FullFrameEnergy~J per frame above idle (\FullFrameEnergyMin--\FullFrameEnergyMax~J). Thresholding, the temporal policy and event logging add no measurable GPU energy, consistent with the sub-millisecond policy step reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}. Unpaced, the model alone reaches \InferMaxFps~FPS and the full pipeline \FullMaxFps~FPS. Median per-frame latency at \BenchFps~FPS is \FullLatencyMs~ms, comparable to the \PaperAVisionLatency~ms vision stage reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, whose \PaperALatency~ms end-to-end cycle additionally includes CPU-side PNG decoding, an optical check and sensor processing that our GPU measurement does not cover. With the $P_{host}$ allowance, one edge cell draws a few tens of watts. That corresponds to $E_{edge}$ between \PrecEdgeKWh{} and \HiValEdgeKWh~kWh per FU, depending on how long the line takes to produce one FU.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Regime Comparison}
Table~\ref{tab:regimes} and Fig.~\ref{fig:regimes} summarise the six regimes at central parameter values. Relative to manual inspection, the full policy B3 reduces carbon by \PrecRelCarbonReduction\%, \MetalRelCarbonReduction\% and \HiValRelCarbonReduction\% in scenarios A, B and C ($\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsLZero~\kgce{} per FU) and reduces unrecovered material ($\Delta M=\PrecDeltaMvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaMvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaMvsLZero~kg). It uses \emph{more} electricity ($\Delta E=\PrecDeltaEvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaEvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaEvsLZero$~kWh), almost all of it rework electricity: prompt interception keeps defects reworkable that manual end-of-line inspection finds too late. It also needs more operator time than manual inspection ($\Delta H=\PrecDeltaHvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaHvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaHvsLZero$~h), because every alert, including those caused by glare, takes a full review. Without the incident latch the picture changes completely: single-frame thresholding (B0) produces $\rho=\PrecRhoBZero$, \MetalRhoBZero{} and \HiValRhoBZero{}, i.e.\ it would need \PrecReviewersBZero, \MetalReviewersBZero{} and \HiValReviewersBZero{} reviewers. In scenario~A the resulting workstation electricity makes B0 emit more than manual inspection (\PrecCarbonBZero{} vs \PrecCarbonLZero~\kgce{}). B3 stays below one reviewer in scenarios B and C but needs \PrecReviewersBThree{} in scenario~A ($\rho=\PrecRhoBThree$), whose defect rate exceeds the roughly \PaperALoadCross{} defect episodes per hour that~\cite{sengar2026paperA} found one reviewer can absorb.

\subsection{What Drives the Carbon Benefit}
The waterfall in Fig.~\ref{fig:waterfall} decomposes $\Delta C$ (B3 vs L0). Avoided field escapes contribute \PrecEscapeShare\%, \MetalEscapeShare\% and \HiValEscapeShare\%, followed by avoided unrecovered material; rework electricity is the largest negative term. Edge electricity and amortised edge hardware together amount to \PrecEdgeCarbon, \MetalEdgeCarbon{} and \HiValEdgeCarbon~\kgce{} per FU---\PrecEdgeOfBenefit\%, \MetalEdgeOfBenefit\% and \HiValEdgeOfBenefit\% of the benefit and at most \EdgeShareMax\% of B3's total footprint. The compute side of the debate is smaller by more than two orders of magnitude. Recall, and what an escaped defect costs, decide the outcome.

\subsection{Break-Even Frontiers}
Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty} and Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven} report where $\Delta C=0$. Against no inspection, the edge cell pays back its electricity, hardware and review carbon once prevalence exceeds \PrecPiStarNZero, \MetalPiStarNZero{} and \HiValPiStarNZero~ppm. Against manual inspection the frontier lies at \PrecPiStarLZero, \MetalPiStarLZero{} and \HiValPiStarLZero~ppm. Holding prevalence at its central value, the edge cell could draw up to \PrecCellPowerStar, \MetalCellPowerStar{} and \HiValCellPowerStar~kW---\PrecCellHeadroom{} to \HiValCellHeadroom{} times the measured value---before the benefit over manual inspection vanishes. No break-even exists for grid intensities up to 1.5~kg/kWh, a range that covers all national grids. Nor does one exist for manual-inspection recall: even perfect manual recall leaves the AI regime ahead, because end-of-line discovery comes too late for rework. Net-negative regimes do exist, but only at part-per-million defect rates.

\subsection{Uncertainty and Global Sensitivity}
Across \MonteCarloDraws{} draws of all \UncertainParams{} uncertain parameters, B3 beats manual inspection in every draw of every scenario, with median $\Delta C$ of \PrecMcMedian, \MetalMcMedian{} and \HiValMcMedian~\kgce{} (5th--95th percentiles in Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty}; Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, left). The 95th percentile of the edge share of B3's footprint is \PrecMcEdgeShareHigh\%, \MetalMcEdgeShareHigh\% and \HiValMcEdgeShareHigh\%. The PRCC ranking (Fig.~\ref{fig:prcc}) is led by defect prevalence, part mass and material factor, the escape consequences ($c_{ret}$, $\kappa$), the manual-inspection recall and the detector recall; the top coefficients are $\PrecTopPrcc$, $\MetalTopPrcc$ and $\HiValTopPrcc$. All edge-cell parameters---GPU and host power, hardware embodied carbon and lifetime---have $|\mathrm{PRCC}|\le\EdgePrccMax$. Grid intensity acts mainly through rework electricity, which B3 increases, so its coefficient is negative. In scenario~A the return-logistics term $c_{ret}$ ranks first because the part itself carries little embodied carbon. Better data on escape consequences would narrow the uncertainty far more than better compute measurements.

\label{fig:prcc}

\subsection{Alert Policy, Workload and the Recall Margin}
B0--B3 share the same edge cell, so differences among them isolate the alert policy. Smoothing alone (B1) removes most false alerts on good parts, but it raises glare alerts, and neither B1 nor persistence without the latch (B2) changes the roughly 150 alerts each defect raises (Table~\ref{tab:policies}); their operator hours differ by at most \BOneBTwoHoursDiffMax\%. The incident latch of B3 collapses repeat alerts to about one per defect. Relative to B0, B3 saves \PrecDeltaHvsBZero, \MetalDeltaHvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaHvsBZero~operator hours and \PrecDeltaEvsBZero, \MetalDeltaEvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaEvsBZero~kWh per FU, and $\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsBZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsBZero~\kgce{}. The Monte Carlo analysis confirms the carbon saving in \PrecMcProbBZero\%, \MetalMcProbBZero\% and \HiValMcProbBZero\% of draws. Two effects limit it. First, the persistence delay costs reworkability where it decays fast: in scenario~C smoothing alone emits slightly less than B3 ($\Delta C=\HiValDeltaCvsBOne$~\kgce{}). Second, any recall that persistence loses turns into field escapes. The companion study measured no such loss, but a deployment may differ, so we solve for the recall loss $\delta_r^\star$ at which B3's advantage over B0 vanishes (Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, right): \PrecRecallLossStar, \MetalRecallLossStar{} and \HiValRecallLossStar{} percentage points. For lightweight parts the margin is wide; for high-value parts, temporal filtering must preserve recall to within about one point to remain carbon-beneficial.

\subsection{Multi-Criteria Index}
Fig.~\ref{fig:sqi} shows the sub-indicators of B3 against L0. Material and carbon improve, whereas electricity ($S_E=\PrecSE$, $\MetalSE$ and $\HiValSE$) and operator time ($S_H=\PrecSH$, $\MetalSH$ and $\HiValSH$) worsen. The balanced SQI is $\PrecSqiBal$, $\MetalSqiBal$ and $\HiValSqiBal$, and it is positive for \PrecSqiRobust\%, \MetalSqiRobust\% and \HiValSqiRobust\% of all possible weightings. A single index hides a genuine conflict: stakeholders who weight electricity or operator time heavily can rank manual inspection higher even though it emits more carbon. We recommend reporting the sub-indicators and the weight-robustness share, not one score.

\section{Discussion}
\emph{Implications.} For the configurations studied, the compute footprint of edge inspection is not the decision variable. A laptop-class GPU at line rate sits more than two orders of magnitude below the quality-driven flows. With break-even prevalences in the part-per-million range, the ``AI is not green'' regime requires near-zero-defect lines or edge cells drawing hundreds to thousands of times more power. The levers that matter are recall, interception time and alert design. Recall and interception time set escapes and reworkability; alert design decides whether the operator queue is feasible at all, and its workstation electricity can outweigh the scrap savings of a lightweight part. Practitioners should spend their measurement effort on escape consequences, on recall under their own defect distributions and on alert rates, not on inference energy.

\emph{Threats to validity.} (i) Most parameters outside the alert policies are scenario assumptions (Table~\ref{tab:parameters}). The results are conditional on them, and the uncertainty and break-even analyses show how the conclusions shift. (ii) The alert rates come from simulated workloads in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, with synthetic glare and sensor channels; the glare rate is an assumption, and alerts per defect were measured on 2--8~s defect episodes and are applied unchanged regardless of how long a part stays in view. The detector recall $r_{AI}$ and the persistence recall loss are assumptions, which is why we report the recall margin. (iii) We measured only GPU power. Host, camera and lighting enter through $P_{host}$, which leaves the conclusions unchanged even at its upper bound. The GPU also served the host desktop under WSL2, and NVML sensors have documented sampling limitations~\cite{yang2024accurate}; long paced windows, repeats and robust statistics mitigate these effects without removing them. (iv) The detector uses random weights and synthetic frames. Production models of similar architecture cost about the same, but larger backbones, multi-camera cells or higher frame rates scale $E_{edge}$ proportionally. Even a 100-fold increase stays below the frontiers of Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven}. (v) Reworkability decay, the detect-and-divert architecture, the single-reviewer queue and the replacement-based escape model are simplifications, and rebound effects and end-of-life treatment lie outside the boundary. (vi) We sample parameters independently, ignoring correlations such as that between part mass and material factor.

\section{Conclusion}
At line rate, a PatchCore-style edge inspection pipeline draws about \FullTotalPower~W on the GPU. Even with host power and hardware added, the edge cell accounts for well under 1\% of the carbon benefit it enables over manual inspection. Edge AI inspection is carbon-beneficial across the uncertainty space we studied; its net-negative regime is confined to part-per-million defect rates. The benefit rests on recall and on what escaped defects cost. Alert design matters more than compute: with measured alert rates, single-frame thresholding is operationally infeasible, while a policy with an incident latch saves operator time, electricity and carbon as long as its temporal filtering keeps recall within a margin that is about one percentage point for high-value parts. All code, raw power traces, the parameter ledger and the scripts that generate every figure, table and number in this paper are available at \url{https://github.com/sengarutk/sustainable-edge-quality-intelligence} under the MIT license.
